# Typography

Figma: [Typography](https://www.figma.com/design/a7Z956YZy9n6f9uz5DK16Y?node-id=69-880)

Syntropy uses a single font family (IBM Plex Sans / IBM Plex Sans Arabic) with two language modes. The system provides 19 sizes, 9 weights, 19 line-heights, and 4 letter-spacings - composed into 37 named text styles ranging from caption/9 to display/72.

## Type System Overview

Syntropy typography uses a single variable font family - Font/Family/Base - that resolves differently per language mode. In English mode it is IBM Plex Sans; in Arabic mode it is IBM Plex Sans Arabic. Designers work with one binding; the system handles the language switch.

- 19 sizes spanning 9px to 72px - the smallest reserved for fine-print only, the largest for marketing displays
- 9 weights from Thin to Black - but in product UI we only use Regular, Medium, SemiBold, and Bold
- 19 line-heights, one matching each size in pixels - never use unitless ratios in Figma, they cannot bind to variables
- 4 letter-spacings - Normal (default), Tight (large display), Snug (modest tightening), Wide (small uppercase labels)
- 37 named text styles compose these primitives into ready-to-use styles like body / 16 / regular, heading / 22 / semibold, display / 48 / bold

## Font Families

Syntropy uses the IBM Plex family - a comprehensive, open-source font family from IBM. The Sans variants ship for both Latin and Arabic scripts with matching x-heights and proportions, which makes mode-switching feel coherent rather than jarring.

## Line Heights

Line-height is stored as a pixel value matching each font size - never as a ratio. Figma cannot bind ratio values to variables, so we use pixel values that produce a consistent ratio: English ≈ 1.43× the font size, Arabic ≈ 1.5×. The Arabic ratio is slightly larger because Arabic glyphs have deeper descenders and require more vertical breathing room.

## Letter Spacing

Four letter-spacing tokens. Most product UI uses Normal (0%). Tight is reserved for large display headings where default tracking looks too loose. Snug is a subtle tightening for marketing headings. Wide is for small uppercase labels (e.g. ALL-CAPS buttons or section eyebrows) to improve legibility.

| Font/LetterSpacing/Normal letter-spacing 0% | Invest Confidently |
| --- | --- |
| Font/LetterSpacing/Tight letter-spacing -2% | Invest Confidently |
| Font/LetterSpacing/Snug letter-spacing -1% | Invest Confidently |
| Font/LetterSpacing/Wide letter-spacing +4% | INVEST CONFIDENTLY |

### Why typography matters

Typography is the foundation of every screen. Users read words - and how those words feel determines whether the product reads as professional, trustworthy, or amateurish. In financial products like Safqah, where every screen involves numbers, contracts, and decisions about money, type clarity directly affects how confident a user feels about investing.

A typography system removes ambiguity. Without one, every designer picks a slightly different size for body text, every engineer pulls a different line-height from a Slack thread, and every screen ends up slightly off. With one, "body / 16 / regular" means exactly the same thing on every screen - same size, same weight, same line-height, same font family, same letter-spacing. The system encodes the decision once, and everyone uses it.

Syntropy is mode-aware by design. The same token Font/Family/Base resolves to IBM Plex Sans for English text and IBM Plex Sans Arabic for Arabic text. Designers don't pick which font - the system picks based on context. This is essential for a bilingual Saudi product where every screen has English and Arabic versions.

### The Syntropy typography system

Syntropy provides five layers of typography primitives, composed into 37 named text styles.

| Col 1 | Col 2 |
| --- | --- |
| Font Family | One variable: Font/Family/Base. Two modes: English (IBM Plex Sans) and Arabic (IBM Plex Sans Arabic). Both are open-source IBM Plex variants with matching x-heights and proportions so mode switching feels seamless. |
| Sizes (19) | From 9px (fine-print only) to 72px (marketing display). The core product range is 12–28px. Sizes 9–11 are for legal disclaimers and metadata. Sizes 32+ are for marketing pages. |
| Weights (9) | Nine weight tokens defined: Thin, ExtraLight, Light, Regular, Medium, SemiBold, Bold, ExtraBold, Black. Only Regular (400), Medium (500), SemiBold (600), and Bold (700) are used in product UI. The rest are for special marketing displays. |
| Line Heights (19) | One pixel-value line-height per font size. English uses ~1.43× the font size, Arabic uses ~1.5×. The Arabic ratio is larger because Arabic glyphs have deeper descenders. Both modes use the same pixel value in the Variable - Figma resolves the right ratio per language mode. |
| Letter Spacings (4) | Tight, Snug, Normal, Wide. Most product UI uses Normal. Tight for large display headings. Snug for moderate tightening. Wide for small uppercase labels. |

> **Tip:** Designers don't pick individual primitives - they pick text styles. body / 16 / regular handles all five primitives at once. Use the right-side text panel to apply a style; never set font properties manually.

### Choosing the right text style

The 37 styles cover almost every typography need. Here's how to pick the right one.

| Col 1 | Col 2 |
| --- | --- |
| For body text | Default to body / 16 / regular for primary content. Use body / 14 / regular for dense interfaces like data tables or compact lists. Use body / 13 / regular for very tight UI chrome (badges, secondary metadata). Avoid going below 13px for body content. |
| For headings | Use heading / 28 / bold for the largest page-level header. heading / 22 / semibold for section titles. heading / 18 / semibold for subsections. Don't skip sizes randomly - choose based on hierarchy depth, not aesthetic preference. |
| For emphasis | Use medium or semibold to add emphasis within body text. Avoid bold for inline emphasis - it's visually heavy and breaks reading flow. Reserve bold for headings or strong UI affordances like button labels. |
| For numbers and stats | Numerical displays often need their own style. For a hero stat (e.g. an investor's total return), use display / 32 / bold or larger. For inline numbers in tables, body / 14 / medium provides enough emphasis without going bold. |
| For captions and metadata | caption / 12 / regular is the default for helper text, captions, and timestamps. caption / 11 / regular works for tighter spaces. caption / 9 / regular is for legal fine-print only - never for content the user is expected to read. |

> **Tip:** When choosing between two similar styles, pick the smaller one if you're unsure. Designers consistently overscale text, especially headings. Smaller, well-spaced typography reads more confidently and feels more professional.

### Arabic typography considerations

Safqah is an Arabic-first product serving a Saudi audience. While the design system supports English equally, Arabic is the primary reading experience for most users. This shapes several typography decisions.

| Col 1 | Col 2 |
| --- | --- |
| Right-to-left layout | Arabic reads right-to-left. Text alignment, padding, icon positions, and progress indicators all flip in Arabic mode. When designing, always check the Arabic mirror - Figma's variant modes will swap automatically, but custom layouts need manual review. |
| Larger line-height | Arabic glyphs have deeper descenders (ج، ح، خ، ع، غ) and require more vertical space between lines. Syntropy line-heights resolve to ~1.5× the font size in Arabic mode vs ~1.43× in English. Don't fight this - tighter Arabic line-heights look cramped and reduce readability. |
| No italics | Arabic typography traditionally does not have italics. Forced obliques look jarring and amateur. Syntropy doesn't provide italic styles. For emphasis in Arabic, use a heavier weight (Medium or SemiBold) instead. |
| Numeral choice | Arabic supports two numeral systems: Western Arabic (0-9) and Eastern Arabic (٠-٩). Modern Saudi UI conventions use Western Arabic numerals for financial figures, since they're universally understood and reduce cognitive load when scanning. Use Eastern Arabic numerals only when explicitly required (e.g. formal religious or ceremonial content). |
| Mode switching | When a user toggles language preference, the entire interface reflows. The same component swaps font family automatically because we bind to Font/Family/Base, which has both English and Arabic modes defined. Designers don't maintain two parallel font systems. |

> **Tip:** Always test typography in both English and Arabic modes before shipping. Some designs that look balanced in English feel cramped in Arabic, especially with multi-line text. Use Figma's mode-switching to preview both.

### Hierarchy and emphasis

Good typography is about hierarchy - the order in which a user reads things. Size, weight, color, and spacing all contribute to hierarchy. The goal is that a user can scan a screen and understand its structure before reading word one.

| Col 1 | Col 2 |
| --- | --- |
| Use size sparingly | Most screens need only 3-4 size tiers: a page title, section headings, body text, and metadata. More than that fragments the visual hierarchy. Don't use 7 different sizes on a single screen. |
| Weight before size | When you need to emphasize text but don't want it to dominate, change weight before size. body / 16 / semibold reads as emphasized but stays visually consistent with surrounding body / 16 / regular. Jumping to a larger size creates a much louder change. |
| Color as secondary emphasis | Use text/muted for de-emphasis (captions, helper text). Use text/brand/darkest or text/brand/primary (with affordance) for branded emphasis. Don't combine color emphasis with weight emphasis unless the text is genuinely important - over-emphasis loses meaning. |
| White space as hierarchy | Generous spacing around headings creates a hierarchy without making them bigger. A 28px heading with 32px of space above and 16px below reads as more important than the same heading without that breathing room. Spacing is half the typography system. |

> **Tip:** Squint at your screen. Can you tell the structure without reading the words? If yes, the hierarchy works. If no, the typography needs more contrast - but not necessarily more size. Often weight or spacing fixes it.

### Anti-patterns (Don't do this)

Mistakes that break typographic consistency and accessibility. Each one is a recurring pattern observed in design system implementations.

> **Don't:** Don't set font properties manually. If you find yourself opening the right-side text panel and entering "16px / 24px / 400" by hand, you're fighting the system. Pick a named text style instead.

> **Don't:** Don't introduce sizes outside the scale. If you need 17px, the system says use 16px or 18px. Custom sizes create drift and break the variable bindings that engineers rely on.

> **Don't:** Don't use Light, Thin, ExtraBold, or Black in product UI. These weights are reserved for marketing displays. They fail accessibility for body text and look visually heavy for headings.

> **Don't:** Don't use italics. They're visually inconsistent across languages - Arabic doesn't support italics natively, so italic English text mixed with non-italic Arabic looks unbalanced. Use weight (Medium or SemiBold) for emphasis instead.

> **Don't:** Don't use ALL CAPS for body text. It's harder to read, fails some accessibility guidelines, and reads as shouting. Reserve ALL CAPS for very small uppercase eyebrow labels with Letter-Spacing/Wide applied.

> **Don't:** Don't mix font families. Syntropy uses only IBM Plex Sans (and Arabic). Bringing in a second font family - even for accent - breaks the system. If you need visual variety, vary weight or size, not family.

> **Don't:** Don't apply text styles to Arabic content as English. Arabic text needs its language mode set on the variables so the right font family resolves. Don't hard-code IBM Plex Sans onto Arabic text.
